[](https://oss.issuehunt.io/r/piotrwitek/typesafe-actions/issues/230) ## Is your feature request related to a real problem or use-case? The Redux team has released the [Redux Toolkit](https://redux-toolkit.js.org/) library for its v1 release in Oct, 2019. This simplifies implementation scenarios with Redux, and they're encouraging users to adopt it for many scenarios. However, their `Action` type is not fully compatible with `typesafe-actions`. The Redux [documentation](https://redux-toolkit.js.org/usage/usage-with-typescript#createreducer) describes how actions should be able to be used with `createReducer`: ```ts { const increment = createAction('increment') const decrement = createAction('decrement') createReducer(0, { [increment.type]: (state, action) => { // action is any here }, [decrement.type]: (state, action: PayloadAction) => { // even though action should actually be PayloadAction, TypeScript can't detect that and won't give a warning here. } }) } ``` They achieve this by having all their `Action`s extend the `BaseActionCreator` type which adds a `type` property and a `match` function for easier integration with Redux tooling. ```ts interface BaseActionCreator { type: T match(action: Action): action is PayloadAction } ``` [[see code](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux-toolkit/blob/master/src/createAction.ts#L84)] I'm building a library that uses both the Redux Toolkit, and `typesafe-actions`, but I'm concerned that none of the actions I create with `typesafe-actions` will be usable in applications using the official Redux Toolkit. ## Describe a solution including usage in code example Seems like the actions from `typesafe-actions` could extend the same properties the Redux Toolkit does, and we could benefit with interoperability and the better type safety as described by the Redux docs. ## Who does this impact? Who is this for? Users of the Redux Toolkit, or building libraries which should interop with official Redux tooling. This could also positively impact the following issue: https://github.com/piotrwitek/typesafe-actions/issues/214 ---

## Summary
Build a GitHub App bot (similar to Algora.io) that automatically comments on issues with bounty instructions and auto-pays contributors when their PRs are merged.

## Problem
- Users need clear instructions on how to participate in bounties
- Manual payout process is slow and error-prone
- No visibility into who is working on what

## Solution Implemented

### 1. GitHub App Integration
- Created Roxonn Contribution Rewards GitHub App
- Webhook handlers for GitHub events
- Secure signature verification with `@octokit/webhooks`
- Installation token management per repository

### 2. Auto-Comment on Issue Opened
When a new issue is created in a repo with the bot installed:
- Bot posts welcome comment with bounty instructions
- Explains `/bounty <amount> <currency>` command
- Explains `/attempt` command for developers
- Shows "Who's Working on This?" tracker table
- Includes FAQ and submission requirements

### 3. Command Handling
- `/bounty <amount> <currency>` - Creates bounty with payment links
- `/attempt` - Records developer intent, updates tracker
- `@roxonn status` - Shows current bounty status

### 4. Auto-Payout on PR Merge
When a PR with `fixes #<issue>` is merged:
- Bot detects linked issues
- Verifies funded bounty exists
- Checks contributor has wallet connected
- Posts payout confirmation comment
- Triggers blockchain payout within 60 seconds

### 5. Attempt Tracking
- Real-time updates to "Who's Working on This?" table
- Shows developer username, start time, status
- Prevents duplicate work

## Files Created/Modified
- `server/github.ts` - Core bot logic
  - `handleIssueOpened()` - Welcome comment
  - `generateWelcomeComment()` - Comment template
  - `handleBountyCommand()` - Bounty creation
  - `handleAttemptCommand()` - Attempt tracking
  - `handlePullRequestMergedForAutoPayout()` - Auto-pay
- `server/routes/webhookRoutes.ts` - Webhook routing
- `server/config.ts` - GitHub App configuration

## Webhook Events Handled
| Event | Handler | Action |
|-------|---------|--------|
| `issues.opened` | `handleIssueOpened` | Post welcome comment |
| `issue_comment.created` | Command parser | Process /bounty, /attempt |
| `pull_request.closed` (merged) | `handlePullRequestMergedForAutoPayout` | Auto-pay |

## Security Features
- HMAC-SHA256 webhook signature verification
- Idempotency via `x-github-delivery` header
- SSRF protection on GitHub API calls
- Rate limiting (1 command/min/user/issue)

## Testing
- [x] Bot posts welcome comment on new issues
- [x] `/bounty 100 USDC` creates bounty with payment links
- [x] `/attempt` records intent and updates tracker
- [x] PR merge triggers auto-payout
- [x] Webhook signatures validated correctly

[](https://oss.issuehunt.io/r/avajs/ava/issues/928) See: https://github.com/avajs/ava/pull/918#issuecomment-227016238 `after.always` has some issues when used as a cleanup task. Specifically, it won't run if: - There are test failures and `--fail-fast` is used. - There are uncaught exceptions thrown. I've advocated using `.before` or `.beforeEach` to ensure state is clean before running, but that means state is left on disk after the test run. It's easy enough to get around that: ``` js function cleanup() { if (temDirExists()) { removeTempDir(); } } test.before(cleanup); test.after.always(cleanup); ``` Still, it might be nicer if we had a modifier that allowed you to do it a little cleaner: ``` js // runs as before and after test.cleanup(cleanupFn); // runs as beforeEach and after (not sure afterEach makes much sense?) test.cleanupEach(cleanupFn); ``` Or maybe we introduce a `.and` modifier: ``` js test.before.and.after(cleanupFn); test.beforeEach.and.after(cleanupFn); test.beforeEach.and.afterEach(cleanupFn); ``` I think the second gives you a little more flexibility and is clearer without reading the docs. The first is probably simpler to implement (though I don't think the second would be very hard) ---

However the order should be reproducible to debug such interdependencies. Ruby's minitest has a [`--seed` option](https://github.com/seattlerb/minitest#running-your-tests) which can be set on the CLI to control the order. Presumably `.serial` would run in source order. We could consider running test files in a random order as well, though they're already somewhat random because each test file runs in its own process, and because each test file runs in its own process it'd be hard to run them in a deterministic order. **Goals**
- Establish a baseline benchmark suite for all platform API endpoints
- Measure latency (p50, p95, p99), throughput (req/s), and error rate under load
- Identify bottlenecks before they surface in production
- Produce a reproducible report that can be re-run on future builds for regression tracking

**Acceptance Criteria**

**Scope**
- [ ] All endpoints under `/api/` are included in the benchmark suite
- [ ] Each endpoint is tested with realistic payload sizes drawn from production schema
- [ ] Auth-protected routes are benchmarked using a dedicated benchmark test token

**Tool & Setup**
- [ ] Benchmarking tool is configured (e.g. `autocannon`, `k6`, or `wrk`) and committed to the repo under `/benchmarks`
- [ ] A single command (e.g. `npm run benchmark`) runs the full suite against a local or staging server
- [ ] A `.env.benchmark` template is documented so contributors can configure the target host

**Metrics Captured Per Endpoint**
- [ ] p50, p95, p99 latency (ms)
- [ ] Requests per second (peak and sustained)
- [ ] Error rate (%)
- [ ] Time to first byte (TTFB)

**Output**
- [ ] Results are written to `/benchmarks/results/` as JSON and a human-readable markdown summary
- [ ] PR includes the markdown summary in the description

**Regression Gate**
- [ ] CI runs a smoke benchmark (low concurrency) and fails if p99 latency exceeds a defined threshold
- [ ] Threshold values are stored in `/benchmarks/thresholds.json` and are reviewable

inspected.body_excerpt: ## [UI Bug] Unauthorized 'Edit Amount' and 'Delete' buttons visible to non-owners ### Summary On the bounties listing page, the **"Edit Amount"** and **"Delete"** buttons are being rendered for users who do not have administrative permissions over the bounty. While the backend correctly prevents the action (showing an "Unauthorized" message), the buttons should be hidden entirely from the UI for non-authorized users. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Log in to Algora.io. 2. Navigate to the bounties page (e.g., `algora.io/bounties`). 3. Locate a bounty created by another user/org (e.g., the **$2,500 IMAP** bounty). 4. Observe that the "Edit Amount" and "Delete" buttons are visible on the card. 5. ## Le problème du financement OSS

GitHub Sponsors est gratuit et utile, mais limité : juste du recurring sponsorship. Beaucoup de patterns économiques OSS modernes ne sont pas couverts.

Polar.sh étend les options pour les mainteneurs :

- **Recurring sponsors** : abonnement mensuel ou annuel.
- **Premium tiers** : badges Discord, accès privé, support prioritaire.
- **Issue bounties** : un utilisateur veut un bug fixé ? Il met un bounty, un dev le claim.
- **Subscriptions** : monétiser des features premium, des docs avancées.
- **One-time purchases** : pour de gros sponsors ponctuels.

## Comment ça se distingue

GitHub Sponsors = juste du don récurrent. Polar.sh = plateforme de monétisation OSS structurée.

Workflow typique :

1. Vous créez votre repo sur Polar.sh, lié à votre GitHub.
2. Configurez les tiers (free, $5/mois, $50/mois, etc.).
3. Configurez des "deals" sur certaines issues (bounty).
4. Les sponsors paient via Polar, vous recevez les fonds (Stripe Connect).

## Bonus : monétiser les milestones

Vous pouvez vendre des "early access" à une feature en développement. Les sponsors qui paient un tier obtiennent accès anticipé. Cela transforme le développement OSS en un model crowdfunding light.

## Vs alternatives

- **GitHub Sponsors** : gratuit, mais limité en features.
- **Open Collective** : transparence financière forte, idéal pour les collectifs (plusieurs mainteneurs).
- **Patreon** : généraliste, moins adapté à OSS spécifique.
- **Buy Me a Coffee** : très simple, pas de tiers structurés.

Polar.sh est le plus aligné aux workflows dev OSS modernes : intégration GitHub native, payments per-issue, etc.

## Pour qui c'est pertinent

- **Mainteneurs OSS** avec une audience établie (>1k stars).
- **Auteurs de plugins** populaires (Webpack, ESLint, framework plugins).
- **Outils B2B sous licence permissive** qui veulent un modèle de soutien optionnel.

## Limites

- **Pour les très petits projets** : peu d'intérêt avant d'avoir une base d'users sérieuse.
- **Tax compliance** : Polar gère, mais vous devez déclarer les revenus selon votre juridiction.
- **Pricing fees** : Polar prend une commission (~5 % vs 0 % GitHub Sponsors).

## Le contexte 2026

L'OSS sustainable funding est devenu un sujet sérieux : licence drama (Redis, HashiCorp), supply chain concerns, dépendance critique sur des mainteneurs solo non rémunérés. Polar.sh, Open Collective, GitHub Sponsors font partie de la solution.

Si vous maintenez un projet OSS sérieux et avez le confort de monétiser : c'est culturellement accepté en 2026. Les sponsors d'entreprise comprennent qu'investir dans la sustainability de leurs dépendances est rationnel.

Proposing an enhancement for the Speeduino's 2S option. 

A 2S does not lend itself to making MAP readings in the traditional 4S sense. So I am proposing an optional method for 2S,s by generating a pseudo MAP value. 

On the strength of having written a few short lines of code that included an interrupt I thought I might be able to modify the Speeduino 2S code myself but I was wrong. Now I need the help of someone that could embrace the 2S Pseudo Map concept and make the programming enhancements required for a Beta version to test the idea. There is a Bounty.

Where a 4S manifold's pressure is at a minimum when the throttle is closed and the pressure maxis out with the throttle open. A 2S is completely the other way around. Lower crankcase pressure at WOT and Higher crankcase pressure at closed throttle. Even though it has pistons and a crankshaft a 2S is more of a pulse jet than it is a mini me 4S.

The basic idea is to use the existing MAP sensor on the Speeduino board to make an instantaneous pressure measurement at a set crank angle (TDC) for minimum pressure and another at a later crank angle (140 ATDC) to find maximum crankcase pressure. Then calculate the difference and multiply it by 3 ( multiplier to be user changeable).  

TDC and 140 ATDC would be pretty much the same for all 2S's and by changing the multiplication factor the range of the MAP value could be adjusted to something sensible as seen by watching the MAP gauge.

To me this difference seems to give the best indication of mass air flow. With the difference at 65% being about 0.33 bar, 15% 0.20 bar and 5% 0.15 bar at a rough guess. 

If we do something like MAP = (Max - Min) * 3

Then 65% on the pipe would be 0.99 bar
And 15% on the pipe would be 0.60 bar
And 5% on the pipe would be 0.45 bar

The 2S pseudo MAP values look like useful traditional 4S MAP values that Speeduino can use in the normal way and off the pipe situations for the 2S would easily show up as a lower MAP value.     

More detailed background can be found here:- https://speeduino.com/forum/viewtopic.php?f=19&t=2020&start=110 ... Basic background in Posts 28967 and 28959
